issues.legal_issue: A notice sent by registered post to the addressee’s correct address gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of service.
material_facts: The authority stated that it sent the allotment letter by registered post to the applicant’s address and produced dispatch records in support.

The applicant did not controvert that account before the lower authorities, and the High Court relied on the dispatch register in finding that the letter had not been sent to the correct person and address.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have assessed the evidence in light of the rebuttable presumption arising from registered post; the presumption is permissible, not inevitable, and may be rebutted by evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and Section 114 illustration (f) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, support a presumption of service when a notice is sent by registered post to the correct address. The presumption is rebuttable and is not compulsory: Harihar Banerjee v. Ramshashi Roy; Mst. L.M.S. Ummu Saleema v. B.B. Gujral; C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed; Gujarat Electricity Board v. Atmaram Sungomal Poshani; Chief Commissioner of Income Tax (Admn.), Bangalore v. V.K. Gururaj; Poonam Verma v. Delhi Development Authority; Sarav Investment & Financial Consultancy Private Limited v. Llyods Register of Shipping Indian Office Staff Provident Fund; Union of India v. S.P. Singh; Municipal Corporation, Ludhiana v. Inderjit Singh; and V.N. Bharat v. Delhi Development Authority.

predicates.administrative_notice_service_dispute: A dispute arose in an administrative proceeding about whether a notice was served on its recipient.
predicates.notice_sent_by_registered_post: The sender dispatched the notice to the recipient by registered post.
predicates.addressee_address_was_correct: The notice was addressed to the recipient at the recipient’s correct address.

issues.definition: When service is disputed in an administrative proceeding and the sender used registered post to the recipient’s correct address, service is presumed, subject to rebuttal.

issues.legal_issue: Selection through a draw does not itself create an enforceable right to an allotment, and an allotment requiring acceptance does not become effective as a concluded contract without the required acceptance.
material_facts: The applicant was selected for a flat through a draw and was later sent a formal allotment letter.
The allotment letter required the applicant to communicate acceptance and make a payment within the specified period.
The applicant neither communicated acceptance nor made the required payment or executed the hire-purchase agreement.
issues.conclusion: The draw only identified a prospective allottee; it did not confer a right to the flat. In the absence of the required acceptance, no concluded contract arose.
issues.legal_principle: A draw of lots is a method of selection, not an allotment that by itself creates a legal right: Delhi Development Authority v. Pushpendra Kumar Jain. An order does not become effective, and does not create an enforceable right, until communicated: Bachhittar Singh v. State of Punjab; State of Punjab v. Amar Singh Harika; Union of India v. Dinanath Shantaram Karekar; State of West Bengal v. M.R. Mondal; and Laxminarayan R. Bhattad v. State of Maharashtra. Here the allotment also expressly required acceptance, which was not sent.

predicates.public_housing_allotment_proceeding: An authority considered an application for a dwelling under a public housing allotment process.
predicates.selection_was_only_by_draw: The applicant was identified for possible allotment through a draw, without the draw itself completing the allotment.
predicates.required_acceptance_was_not_sent: The selected applicant did not communicate acceptance required by the allotment terms.

issues.definition: In a public housing allotment process, selection only by draw coupled with failure to send required acceptance means no enforceable allotment right arose.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot introduce a new factual case for the first time in a writ proceeding when it was not founded before the lower authority and the opposing party is not given an opportunity to answer it.
material_facts: Before the appellate and revisional authorities, the applicant relied on financial difficulties and did not plead that she had not received the allotment letter.
The applicant first alleged non-receipt of the allotment letter in the writ petition.
The High Court relied on that new factual case without giving the authority a proper opportunity to controvert it or produce supporting material.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the new factual plea in those circumstances; its haste and failure to provide an opportunity to answer the plea were arbitrary.
issues.legal_principle: A pure question of law may be raised at any stage, but a factual or mixed question requiring investigation cannot be raised for the first time in a writ petition without a factual foundation before the lower authority. If a court exceptionally entertains such a new factual plea, it must give the opposing party an opportunity to controvert it and adduce evidence. State of U.P. v. Dr. Anupam Gupta; Ram Kumar Agrawal v. Thawar Das; Vasantha Viswanathan v. V.K. Elayalwar; Anup Kumar Kundu v. Sudip Charan Chakraborty; Tirupati Jute Industries (P) Ltd. v. State of West Bengal; Sanghvi Reconditioners (P) Ltd. v. Union of India; and Fuljit Kaur v. State of Punjab.

predicates.writ_review_of_lower_authority_decision: A court considered a writ petition challenging a decision made by a lower authority.
predicates.factual_plea_first_raised_in_writ: A party first asserted a material factual claim in the writ proceeding, without having raised it before the lower authority.
predicates.opposing_party_given_no_chance_to_answer: The court did not give the opposing party a proper opportunity to respond to the new factual claim and present supporting evidence.

issues.definition: In writ review of a lower authority’s decision, a factual claim first raised in the writ proceeding cannot be relied on when the opposing party has no opportunity to answer it.

issues.legal_issue: Cancellation of an allotment for default may be sustained where the allottee fails to make required payments and complete the required steps without a cogent explanation, although cancellation should be a last resort.
material_facts: The applicant did not respond to the allotment letter, make the required payment, communicate acceptance, or execute the required hire-purchase agreement.

She remained inactive for years and did not provide a cogent explanation for failing to meet the allotment requirements; her revision stated that she could not arrange the funds and later became ready to pay.
The authority cancelled the allotment and forfeited the earnest money under the governing statutory provisions.
issues.conclusion: The cancellation and forfeiture were sustained, and the orders of the statutory authorities were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Cancellation should be a last resort, and the authority should consider whether the allottee’s intention or motive in failing to pay is evident. The power of resumption and forfeiture is nevertheless available in exceptional circumstances, including failure to make payment in accordance with the allotment; sympathy or sentiment cannot justify a result contrary to statutory provisions. Teri Oat Estates (P) Ltd. v. Union Territory of Chandigarh.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_review_of_statutory_allotment_cancellation and authority_had_cancellation_power_for_default and required_payment_was_not_made and required_allotment_steps_were_not_completed and no_cogent_explanation_was_given

predicates.appeal_from_writ_review_of_statutory_all: An appeal challenged a writ court’s review of a statutory authority’s cancellation of an allotment.
predicates.authority_had_cancellation_power_for_def: The governing allotment scheme authorized the authority to cancel for failure to meet the allotment requirements.
predicates.required_payment_was_not_made: The allottee failed to make a payment required by the allotment terms.
predicates.required_allotment_steps_were_not_comple: The allottee failed to complete other required steps, such as communicating acceptance or executing the allotment agreement.
predicates.no_cogent_explanation_was_given: The allottee did not provide a cogent explanation for failing to meet the requirements.

issues.definition: When an allotment-cancellation appeal concerns an authority empowered to cancel for default, and the allottee neither pays nor completes required steps nor gives a cogent explanation, the cancellation and forfeiture are sustained.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court need not remit a writ dispute for reconsideration when it has examined the record and a remand would serve no purpose because of the time already elapsed.
material_facts: The proceedings had been ongoing for a substantial period.
The Supreme Court examined the entire record and reappreciated the evidence while considering the appeal.
issues.conclusion: Rather than remit the matter to the High Court, the Supreme Court decided the appeal on the record before it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered remittal but concluded that it would serve no purpose given the elapsed time and its own examination of the entire record; no earlier case was cited for this case-management conclusion.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_judgment: An appellate court considered an appeal from a judgment in a writ proceeding.
predicates.substantial_time_has_elapsed: A substantial period passed during the proceedings before the appeal was decided.
predicates.appellate_court_has_examined_entire_reco: The appellate court examined the complete record and reappreciated the evidence.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a writ judgment, substantial elapsed time and the appellate court’s examination of the entire record support deciding the dispute without remand.
